chief_complaint: severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody stools in elderly
hpi_details: A 73-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody stools. The symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he might have picked up a severe bout of food poisoning from some spoiled seafood he ate over the weekend.
concerns: He is worried that this sudden rectal bleeding means he has colon cancer, which is what his older brother died from.
expectations: He hopes to get medicine to relieve the severe cramping and reassurance that he will not need an emergency hospital admission today.

investigation_events.title: Urgent ischemic colitis results
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent laboratory and CT results are now available; IV fluids, bowel rest, and early specialist consultation should not be delayed.

results.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
results.value: Segmental wall thickening and submucosal edema centered at the splenic flexure with reduced enhancement; no pneumatosis or free air

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ischemic Colitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes ordering urgent CT angiography of the abdomen, starting IV fluids, and placing the bowel on rest, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody stools in elderly

Key HPI features: A 73-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody stools. The symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ischemic Colitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ischemic Colitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Inflammatory bowel disease flare without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Known atrial fibrillation with acute abdominal pain and bloody stools — raises suspicion for bowel ischaemia.
management_principles: Order urgent CT angiography of abdomen, start IV fluids, place bowel on rest
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody stools in elderly. HPI: hypoperfusion of colon, atrial fibrillation.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ischemic Colitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Ischemic Colitis.
reference_soap.plan: Assess hemodynamic stability and obtain CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast. Provide IV fluids and bowel rest, with early gastroenterology/surgical consultation when severe disease is suspected. Obtain CT angiography urgently if pain is disproportionate or embolic risk suggests acute mesenteric ischemia.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Ischemic Colitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Ischemic Colitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order urgent CT angiography of abdomen, start IV fluids, place bowel on rest

teaching.one_liner: Reduced blood flow to the colon, often from an irregular heartbeat, damages its lining and causes sudden crampy abdominal pain with bloody stools.
red_flags: Known atrial fibrillation with acute abdominal pain and bloody stools — raises suspicion for bowel ischaemia

must_ask.say: Did the cramping start before the bloody stools appeared?
Do you have an irregular heartbeat, or take blood thinners?
What colour is the blood — bright red, or darker and mixed with the stool?
Where exactly is the pain, and how severe is it?
Do you have any circulation problems or heart disease?
Have you had any fever with this?

history.answer: I've had severe cramping pain in my belly since yesterday, and this morning I started passing bloody stools.
The cramps started suddenly about twenty-four hours ago and have been steadily getting worse.
The severe cramping belly pain hit me first, and then about six hours later I had urgent bloody diarrhea.
It is mainly on the lower left side of my belly, and it has stayed in that same spot without shifting.
No, the pain stays right in my lower abdomen and does not shoot into my back, chest, or groin.
It feels like sharp, twisting cramps that come in waves every few minutes.
It is quite severe, about a seven or eight out of ten when a cramping wave hits.
Nothing really relieves it, and pressing on my belly or trying to eat anything makes the cramping worse.
No, I have never had severe abdominal pain or bloody stools like this in my life.
I felt slightly nauseated from the intense pain, but I haven't thrown up.
I have had three loose bowel movements today, and each time the stool was dark red and maroon with small clots.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats.
No yellowing of my skin or eyes, and my urine looks normal pale yellow.
No pain or burning with urination, and I am not going to the bathroom to pee any more often than usual.
I feel worn out and generalized fatigue, with slight lightheadedness when standing up quickly, but I haven't passed out.
No chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath at all.
I had simple chicken soup and rice yesterday, nothing greasy or spoiled, and no alcohol.
No, I do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, or any other pain relievers.
My heart occasionally flutters or skips beats in my chest, and a doctor once told me my pulse was irregular, but I was never placed on medication for it.
I have not been diagnosed with peripheral artery disease or diabetes, though a doctor previously mentioned slightly borderline blood pressure.
I was wondering if I just caught a terrible case of food poisoning from some spoiled fish I ate a couple of days ago.
I'm terrified that this bleeding means I have colon cancer, which is what my older brother passed away from.
I'm hoping you can give me something to stop this awful cramping and let me know if I can safely go home to rest.
Aside from that occasional irregular fluttering heartbeat, I have had no major medical diagnoses.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked in my life.
I am only a social drinker, having an occasional beer or glass of wine once or twice a month.
I am a retired high school teacher and live at home with my wife.
My father had heart issues in his late seventies, but there is no family history of colon cancer or inflammatory bowel disease.

exam.finding: Elderly male lying on the examination table, appearing mildly fatigued and uncomfortable from abdominal cramping, but alert and oriented.
Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, pulse 90 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.9°C.
Conjunctivae show mild pallor; sclerae are clear and non-icteric.
Irregularly irregular heart rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without distension, caput medusae, or surgical scars.
Hyperactive bowel sounds heard across all quadrants; no abdominal aortic or renal bruits appreciated.
Mild to moderate localized tenderness upon palpation in the left lower quadrant and left flank, with mild voluntary guarding but no abdominal rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited; abdomen remains soft overall.
Murphy sign is negative with no tenderness or inspiratory arrest in the right upper quadrant.
McBurney point tenderness is absent, and psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Normal anal sphincter tone with no palpable anorectal masses; dark red maroon blood mixed with loose stool is present on the examining glove.
